blocks.x: Two weeks is the perfect amount of time for first-time visitors to Japan.

I love this country, and it has so much to offer its guests. With so many incredible places to check off, however, planning an all-encompassing itinerary can get more than a little overwhelming. Should you stick to the classic Tokyo-Kyoto-Osaka triangle? Is Hiroshima worth visiting or is Mount Fuji a waste of time? Do the infamous levels of overtourism mean you should focus on lesser-known spots instead? And how on earth are you supposed to see everything within two weeks?
You have questions, I have answers!

I had a fantastic first visit to Japan and am determined to make sure your time in the country ends up being just as magical as mine. I would recommend this itinerary to anyone who is heading to the country — and as I write this post, my parents are currently in Tokyo, about to start following my exact route.

With two weeks, you’ll be able to experience the very best of this country without spending your entire trip navigating your way through a seemingly endless number of gigantic train stations. You’ll see Japan’s biggest cities, experience its traditional neighbourhoods, eat an unreasonable amount of excellent food, and still have time to explore the country’s quieter side. There’ll be mountains and megacities, neon-lit streets and silent temple courtyards, ferries and trains, and more convenience store snacks than you ever thought possible.
You’ll have to trust me on that last point: the convenience stores in this country are on a whole other level!

Below, you’ll find a brief overview of my two-week itinerary, then I’m going to break everything down by day, explaining exactly what to do in each place, why it’s worth visiting, where to stay, and how to maximise your time in town.

Day One: Get Your Bearings in Shibuya

blocks.x: My friend, you’re finally here. Welcome to one of the most beloved cities in the world.

Are you already feeling overwhelmed? If so, take a deep breath and know that you’re not alone. This chaotic megacity is vast, crowded, and dizzying, so the initial culture shock can leave you feeling more than a little disoriented. Never fear: you’ll soon adjust to Tokyo’s vibe and it’s not as intense as first impressions might have you believing.

I always recommend that first-time visitors to the city kick off their explorations in Shibuya. In my opinion, this neighbourhood provides the perfect introduction to travel in Japan, predominantly because it’s most likely home to the scenes you’ve been picturing when imagining visiting this country.

Yes, Shibuya is energetic, colourful, hipster, and touristy, home to towering buildings, flashing billboards, cool boutiques, and peaceful shrines and backstreets, all packed into a handful of city blocks. Oh, and it’s also home to one of the most iconic pedestrian crossings in the world. We’ll head there almost immediately after arriving.

First though, start your explorations at the Hachiko Statue, which is located directly outside of Shibuya train station. Oh, and I have to mention here that Shibuya station may just be one of the most baffling in the world to navigate (speaking as somebody who once spend 40 minutes simply trying to exit the station!) Look for signs for the Hachiko Exit if you’re arriving from a JR Train, or Hachiko Gate followed by Exit 8 if you’re arriving via the subway.
So who is Hachiko?

Hachiko is actually a dog, and he’s beloved by residents of the city. Hachiko’s owner was a professor at the University of Tokyo, and every single afternoon, the dog would wait for him to arrive at Shibuya Station so they could walk home together. When the professor unexpectedly died, Hachiko continued to return to the station every single day for the next 10 years, always looking for him. No, you’re crying!

Once you’ve paid your respects to the most loyal of companions, it’s time to dive straight into the organised chaos of Shibuya Crossing. You can see it from the statue, but if you’ve somehow managed to get lost already, or started your itinerary from a different location, you’ll find it by searching for Shibuya Scramble Crossing on Google Maps.
And what a scramble it is.

This is most likely the busiest pedestrian intersection in the world, with up to 3,000 people crossing the street at once whenever the lights turn green. It’s so much fun to experience, so I recommend crossing multiple times to get a feel for the flow of the city.

It offers a great insight into Japan’s organisational skills, too: despite the sheer number of people on the ground, everyone still manages to wait calmly for the lights and walk without colliding into each other. It looks like madness from the outside, but when you’re in the midst of it, it’s surprisingly orderly.
If you want an elevated view of the crossing (and you definitely do), you’ve got a few options.

The classic viewpoint comes from the nearby Starbucks, and you can see how the crossing will look from my photo above. It’s one the cheapest options, as you only need to buy a coffee, but the downsides are that it’s far from undiscovered (so don’t expect to get a seat directly beside the window) and you don’t get the see the crossing from up high.

The viewpoint I’d recommend most, though, is Shibuya Sky and I’d specifically recommend booking through Klook (as they’re often cheaper while also allowing you to cancel up to a day before, which is useful if the weather isn’t so great.) This is my favourite observation deck in Tokyo, and so if you’re going to do just one, make it Shibuya Sky.

At 229 metres above Tokyo, its open-air rooftop gives you a real sense for just how absolutely gigantic this city is. You’ve got Shibuya Crossing directly below and thousands of skyscrapers stretching into the distance. On a clear day, you can usually spot the two other famous observation decks in the city, Tokyo Tower and Tokyo Skytree, and if it’s an exceptionally clear day, you can see as far as Mount Fuji.

After taking in the views, wander through Center-Gai and Koen-Dori streets. These bustling lanes are full of street fashion, quirky boutiques, and vibrant energy that gives you a true taste of contemporary Tokyo culture. Shibuya 109 is perfect if shopping and fashion are your priorities. You can easily spend a few hours weaving between these areas.

Tower Records is fun to visit for a hefty dose of nostalgia, and if you discover you’ve forgotten to pack anything in your luggage, this is the perfect area for shopping. I may have spent this first day replacing my well-worn travel closet with Japanese versions.

In the afternoon, take a gentle breather. If you’re starting to feel the effects of travel, relax in a small cafe or return to your hotel briefly. High-energy travellers can continue exploring Shibuya’s backstreets, including Dogenzaka alleyways and Nonbei Yokocho, a labyrinth of narrow lanes with tiny bars, bakeries, and izakayas that feel like hidden Tokyo treasures. Cat Street between Harajuku and Shibuya offers a quieter experience and independent shopping, providing a calmer contrast to the main tourist areas.

Where to stay in Tokyo: It’s your first day in Japan! And so, it makes sense to really throw yourself into the local experience. That’s why we decided to stay at this lovely onsen-ryokan in Shinjuku. (Whenever readers ask me which neighbourhood to choose in Tokyo, I always recommend Shinjuku or Shibuya.) The reason why I loved this specific property, though, is because it’s a ryokan (traditional Japanese Inn) that also has an onsen (hot pool). It’s a great way to jump immediately into all things Japanese.

And it was wonderful; one of my favourite hotels in the country. The rooms were small and cosy, and felt super-traditional and calming. The views over Tokyo at night from the window were incredible. And the rooftop onsen? With free popsicles afterwards? So good. It’s located in a quieter neighbourhood, but still only a 10-minute walk to the subway. I really recommend this one!
Wake up ready to dive into Tokyo’s youthful, creative energy because today is all about Harajuku and Omotesando, where fashion, cafes, and street art all reign supreme.

Start your morning at Meiji Jingu, tucked behind Harajuku Station. Enter through the towering Torii gate and follow the gravel paths through a forested oasis that feels miles away from the city chaos. Pause to watch locals perform rituals, snap a few photos, or catch a traditional wedding procession weaving through the grounds.
Once you leave the shrine, head out for brunch at a cafe I love to recommend: Mr Farmer for fresh, Instagram-worthy dishes, or Deus Ex Machina for excellent coffee.

Next, wander through Takeshita Street. Yes, it’s touristy, but it’s iconic. Rainbow crepes, quirky fashion boutiques, and people-watching that’s impossible to beat. Don’t stick to the main drag. Duck into the side streets. Vintage shops, indie sneaker stores, and tiny galleries hide everywhere. Big Love Records is a must if you love vinyl. Small independent brands in these alleyways are shaping Harajuku’s ever-changing street style.

By mid-morning, wander over to Omotesando, Harajuku’s quieter, polished sibling. Wide boulevards, modern architecture, luxury stores, and stunning window displays. Pause for a coffee at a minimalistic cafe. Admire the Prada building or duck into the Design Festa Gallery for a dose of creative chaos. Omotesando is where Harajuku’s street culture meets high design.
Lunch can be casual and fun. Explore Ura-Harajuku for hidden ramen shops, trendy burgers, or sushi cafes that feel like local secrets.

By late afternoon, shift the pace to Shinjuku. Start at the Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building for sunset. Free observation decks give sweeping city views, and on clear days you can spot Mount Fuji.

There’s one place that everyone heads to after spending time in Shinjuku, and it has two very different names, evoking two very different images: Memory Lane a.k.a Piss Alley! This is a particularly aesthetic part of the neighbourhood, and is famed for its teeny-tiny eateries serving yakitori and cheap beer. The narrow street is usually decorated for the season (you can see the autumn colours from my trip above) and makes for some excellent photos.

There’s no hiding it, however: this is unmistakably a part of town that’s designed for tourists. You’ll rarely see locals hanging out and eating due to the higher prices (and mandatory cover charge at most places), but it also is a great place to go if you’re new to Japan and feeling intimidated by the food. The menus will likely be in English, you won’t have to worry about whether you’ll be welcome inside or not, so it’s sort-of like a beginners guide to eating at an Izakaya.

Okay, time for some definitions! An izakaya is the name given to a Japanese pub: they’re usually super-small and cosy, and offer bar snacks and beers to patrons. Often those snacks will be yakitori, which is basically grilled meat and vegetables on a stick. You can go all-out here and try some truly interesting dishes: Dave and I are adventurous eaters so opted for chicken gizzards, chicken liver, and chicken heart, but you can just as easily find breast and thigh, as well as vegetables.
Day Three: Head Over to Central Tokyo

Wake up feeling ready for a mix of history, gardens, architecture, and shopping. Today is Central Tokyo, where you get to see a different side of the city: quieter, elegant, and full of unexpected charm.

Start your morning at the Imperial Palace. The East Gardens are open to the public and are the perfect place to wander slowly. Gravel paths, meticulously maintained lawns, and seasonal flowers make it feel almost otherworldly. Don’t miss the remains of old Edo Castle walls and moats — they’re a glimpse into Japan’s feudal past right in the middle of the modern city. Pause on the stone bridges for photos, and notice the contrast between the peaceful gardens and the skyscrapers peeking above the trees.

From there, stroll along Nijubashi Bridge. It’s the postcard-perfect spot for the classic Imperial Palace photo. Watch the guards march by, the occasional ceremonial horse, and take a deep breath — it’s surprisingly serene considering you’re just a 10-minute walk from Tokyo Station.

Next, wander towards Marunouchi, the district that blends business, shopping, and architecture seamlessly. Tokyo Station’s red brick exterior is stunning, and inside you can explore the station’s underground shopping malls. Grab a coffee or a sweet treat from one of the artisanal cafes tucked away in the station complex. This is a good chance to fuel up before the day accelerates.

If you’re into art, the Mitsubishi Ichigokan Museum is nearby. Housed in a restored Meiji-era building, it’s small but filled with rotating exhibitions of European and Japanese art. Even if you only pop in for 20 minutes, it’s worth the step into history.

For lunch, Marunouchi and Ginza are packed with options. Head to Marunouchi Brick Square or one of the department store food halls for an elegant bento, sushi, or tempura set. Or, for something different, try Kyubey in Ginza — it’s high-end sushi but an institution if you want a quick but memorable meal.

After lunch, start exploring Ginza on foot. Skip the main avenue for a bit and wander the back streets where tiny galleries, independent designer shops, and charming cafes hide. Check out Itōya, the legendary stationery store with floors and floors of pens, papers, and Japanese notebooks. Even if you’re not a stationery nerd, the displays are hypnotic. If you’re feeling cultural, Ginza Six has an art space and a rooftop garden with great city views.

By mid-afternoon, wander toward Nihonbashi. This historic commercial district is where Tokyo started as a city. The iconic Nihonbashi Bridge, local craft shops, and department stores like Mitsukoshi are perfect for a slower-paced exploration. Stop for matcha or wagashi in one of the traditional tea houses.

As evening approaches, circle back to Ginza for the lights. This area transforms at night: street lamps, illuminated store fronts, and quiet alleys make it feel elegant and cinematic. Treat yourself to dessert at one of Ginza’s famous patisseries or cafés. For a slightly lively evening, visit one of the rooftop bars for a nightcap and views over the glittering city streets.

Optional detours if you have energy: pop into the Sony Building to check out the latest tech demos, or walk to nearby Yurakucho for more hidden alleys of izakayas and old-school theatres. If it’s museum day, the Bank of Japan Currency Museum is free and oddly fascinating.
Day Four: Get Your Geek On in Akihabara

Start your morning bright and early in Asakusa, one of Tokyo’s most charming historic districts. The star here is Senso-ji, Tokyo’s oldest temple. Arrive early to beat the crowds and soak in the atmosphere: the towering Kaminarimon gate, the giant red lantern, and the bustling Nakamise Street lined with traditional snacks and souvenirs. Don’t just rush — try freshly made ningyo-yaki (little cakes shaped like dolls) or pick up a quirky charm from one of the tiny shops.

Wander around the temple grounds for a while. There’s a peacefulness here that contrasts beautifully with the vibrant streets outside. You can also explore the nearby Asakusa Culture and Tourist Center for a free observation deck overlooking the temple and the surrounding streets. It’s a great spot to plan your next move and snap some photos from above.

From Asakusa, it’s a short walk or ride to Sumida Park along the river. If it’s cherry blossom season, this is a stunning spot. Even outside of spring, the park offers calm paths, riverside views, and photo opportunities with the Tokyo Skytree looming nearby. For something a little quirky, visit the Edo-Tokyo Museum (just a short train ride away) to see fascinating exhibits on Tokyo’s transformation from Edo-era streets to the neon megacity it is today.

Lunch options in this area are endless. For a local classic, try tempura at Daikokuya or unagi (grilled eel) at one of the riverside restaurants. If you’re feeling adventurous, explore street food stalls in Asakusa: taiyaki, melon pan, or skewers of all kinds. Grab a cold drink and wander — the neighborhood rewards curiosity.

Once you’ve had your fill, head to Ueno. Ueno Park is a sprawling green oasis with museums, temples, and a zoo. The Tokyo National Museum is a must for a crash course in Japanese art, archaeology, and history. Even if you only spend an hour, you’ll see samurai armour, ceramics, and ancient scrolls.
By mid-afternoon, make your way to Akihabara. Brace yourself, as this neighbourhood can be overwhelming!

Akihabara used to be Tokyo’s electronics district and while you can still find plentiful technology stores there — Dave bought a new shaver there! — it’s now also the home of manga madness. In short, this neighbourhood is bright, noisy, and jam-packed with comic book stores. It’s the perfect place to spend an afternoon people-watching, experiencing culture shock, and pondering how it’s possible for so much neon to exist in one place.

Dive into the manga and anime stores, where there’s everything from new releases to retro collectibles. Super Potato is legendary for retro games; even if you don’t buy anything, it’s a trip down gaming history. Maid cafes are infamous here; visiting one is optional, but walking past and watching the cosplay energy is a spectacle in itself.

If you want a twist, sign up for themed go-karting tours where you drive through Tokyo dressed as a Nintendo or anime character. It sounds crazy — and it is — but it’s the kind of unforgettable experience that makes Akihabara unique.

As evening sets in, explore the backstreets for tiny bars, snack shops, and quirky street performances. Take a breather at a cafe or arcade, or wander until the neon lights feel like they’re alive around you.
This part of the city is exactly what you’re imagining when you think of Tokyo.
Day Five: Mount FUJI OR NIKKO
Volcanoes or shrines? Fuji or Nikko?

That’s the choice you’ll be making for day five, as there’s two main options for overnight stays (or day trips) from Tokyo. I’ve been to both Hakone (the main base for exploring Fuji) and Nikko (a countryside town that’s jam-packed with forest temples and shrines), and I’d say that if you’re not sure which one to choose, make your decision based on the time of year you’ll be in town.

The reality is that it is unbelievably rare to see Mount Fuji against a blue-sky backdrop. Numbers show that this ancient volcano is clearly visible for just 80 days a year on average, so the odds are most definitely not in your favour. The time of year makes a huge difference, too: last year, Fuji was visible for 80% of February, while the numbers plummeted to just 7% of June!

Visiting Hakone in autumn and winter, therefore, gives you the best odds, but there’s still a chance you could rock up and not be able to see it at all! We visited Mount Fuji in December and I complained about the cloudy weather at the time with no idea just how lucky we were.
So what about Nikko?

If you’re visiting in spring or summer, Nikko is a much safer bet, weather-wise. This historic mountain town is surrounded by dense forest, waterfalls, and so many temples and shrines that it’s hard to see them all in one day. I think it makes for a fun contrast with the rest of the itinerary, too, as it’s unlike anywhere else you’ll visit: deep in the mountainous countryside and full of intricate temples, it felt like wandering through a Japanese fairytale!
(If both appeal, you could cut a day from your time in Tokyo [I’d probably blend the first two days together] to make room for the two of them!)

Getting to Hakone: Hakone is 90 minutes from Tokyo and there’s plenty of options for trains. The easiest option is to buy the Hakone Free Pass, which gives you round-trip train tickets from Shinjuku to Hakone plus unlimited access to all transportation options in Hakone, including the Tozan cable car, ropeway, and sightseeing lake cruise.

Getting to Nikko: If you have a JR Pass, it will cover you for travel between Tokyo and Nikko but takes just over 2 hours and requires you to change at Utsunomiya. We decided to take the Tobu Japan Limited Express train instead, which is direct and takes 1 hour 50 minutes. I’ll warn you in advance that the website is wildly confusing, but here’s exactly what you need to buy: first, get the Nikko Pass World Heritage Area pass, which covers the round-trip basic train fare between Tokyo and Nikko as well as the local buses in Nikko. Then, buy a Limited Express Ticket for each journey, which is essentially an upgrade that lets you take the faster, reserved-seat trains.
I’ll cover Hakone first.

Your Hakone Free Pass will get you from Shinjuku to Hakone-Yumoto, which is the main transportation hub in Hakone. If you’ll be staying overnight in Hakone, like we did, you’ll find luggage storage lockers and a baggage counter. If you drop your luggage off before 10 a.m., they’ll deliver it to your hotel in Hakone by 3 p.m. that afternoon, which is a pretty amazing service!

From Hakone-Yumoto, you’ll ride the Hakone Tozan Railway to Gora on board a wonderfully retro mountain train that slowly climbs its way upwards through the forest. At Gora, head to the Hakone Tozan Cable Car, which will take you even higher to Sounzan. That’s when the spectacular views really start to emerge.

If you can believe it, you’ll be taking another method of transport shortly afterwards: the Hakone Ropeway, although it’s really just another cable car. This one’s more thrilling, though, with the first section whisking you over the enormous volcanic crater of Owakudani. You’ll see neon yellow rocks below with plumes of steam emanating from them, along with a distinct smell of sulphur in the air.

Disembark from the ropeway at Owakudani and get ready to start exploring. This is where you’ll get to try the region’s famous jet-black eggs. They’re regular chicken eggs, but they’ve been boiled in volcanic water, which is what gives the shells their colour. The waters in this part of Japan are rich in iron while the volcanic activity below releases hydrogen sulphide gas. Mix the two together and you get iron sulphide, which is black!

Legend says that eating one of these eggs adds seven years to your life, so I eagerly bought myself a couple. They tasted much the same as a regular boiled egg, but there was a slight sulphur flavour, which made the experience even more… volcanic.
When you’ve finished marvelling at the geothermal landscape in Owakudani, reboard the ropeway and continue onwards towards Togendai, where you’ll be trading mountains for water.

Step aboard the Hakone Sightseeing Cruise across Lake Ashi (appropriately named for a volcanic lake!), which is going to give you an entirely new perspective of the area. And yes, the boats are pirate-themed, which is a little unexpected (they were built after the cruise’s president visited Disneyland and felt inspired to create something similar in Hakone).
Aim to nab a space on the top deck, as it’ll give you a great view of the torii gate of Hakone Shrine with Mount Fuji looming in the distance.

You’ll have two options for where to take the cruise to: Hakone-machi and Moto-Hakone. I recommend the latter, as it has more interesting things to see. The village of Moto-Hakone is home to plenty of cafes and restaurants if you’re feeling hungry. We loved our meal from Hiroshiya, where you can sample the local smelt, caught fresh from the lake.

Walk to Heiwa-no-Torii, the red gate you may have spotted on your cruise, then venture up the stone steps to see the rest of Hakone Shrine. Once you’ve finished exploring, you can catch a bus from Moto-Hakone back to Hakone-Yumoto, where you’ll either get the train back to Tokyo if you’re visiting as a day trip, or collect your backpacks and head to your accommodation if you’re staying overnight.

Where to stay in Hakone: We opted for a room in a lovely guesthouse, with a tatami mat floor to sleep on and a private onsen on-site. It ended up being another one of our favourite stays in Japan! The staff were lovely and there was a restaurant/bar that served up surprisingly great pizzas. It had a cosy and chilled-out atmosphere, with great food and wine, and lots of blankets to snuggle up with as we ate. It was also worth staying here just to experience the private onsen — we got to go in as a couple and spend an hour splashing around and recovering from our active day.
If you’ve decided to head to Nikko instead, you’ll find just as much to do there.

We did it as a day trip, rather than an overnight stay, as most of the accommodation in Nikko was either expensive or tricky to access without a car. We took the 8:09 a.m. train from Asakusa, which got us in to Tobu-Nikko at 10:16 a.m, then took the 4:20 p.m. train back to Tokyo, which arrived at 6:15 p.m. If I could have changed anything about this day, I’d have probably booked an earlier train, as the shrines were crowded by the time we arrived and we only just managed to squeeze in everything we wanted to do before our train back.

The main attraction in Nikko is Toshogu Shrine, which is where I took both of the photos you can see above, so you’ll want to make that your first port of call. Your Nikko pass gives you free rides on the local buses, but Dave and I decided to walk there, as we wanted see some of the village and stop off for coffee along the way. Strong recommendation for Meguri Coffee! This warm and cosy cafe had welcoming staff and excellent coffee and matcha; Dave and I especially appreciated the vegan milks, which are still a rarity in Japan.

After roughly 20 minutes of walking, you’ll reach the bright-red and photogenic Shinkyo bridge. There’s a ridiculous fee you can pay to walk across the bridge, but I wouldn’t recommend it, as the best views are from the bridge that runs alongside it. From there, it’s a simple walk uphill to the impressive Toshogu Shrine.

This complex is absolutely enormous, and I could instantly see why it’s a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Give yourself at least an hour and a half here, because there’s so many ornate buildings to take a look at. Keep an eye out for the famous Three Wise Monkeys, the extravagant Yomeimon Gate, and the tiny carving of a sleeping cat; it’ll be easy to find all three as that’s where crowds tend to gather. We enjoyed the walk through the forest to Tokugawa Ieyasu’s tomb, too, as it was a little quieter.

Outside of Toshogu, I was shocked by how rapidly the crowds dissipate. We went from sharing a temple complex with 5,000 people to roughly five! We wandered over to Futarasan Shrine next. It’s only a few minutes away and, unlike extravagant Toshogu, felt more understated. You’ll want to venture next to Taiyuin, which is accessible through an uphill path through the forest and ended up being one of my favourites, as we had the complex mostly to ourselves.

On your walk back down into town, swing past Rinnoji along the way. The main attraction here is the enormous Three Buddha Hall, but our highlight was the peaceful Shoyo-en Gardens. Neither was a must-visit, to be honest, but you need to walk past them, so you might as well take a look.

One part of Nikko I’d strongly recommend trying to get to is the Kanmangafuchi Abyss, which is where I took the photo at the very top of this section, with the collection of moss-blanketed stone statues sitting in a row. What an unusual sight! This area is a little out of the way, taking 25 minutes to walk there from Shinkyo Bridge, so you’ll want to make sure you have at least 90 minutes before your train back to Tokyo, so you won’t be too rushed.

At Kanmangafuchi Abyss, you’ll find over 70 of these stone Jizo statues: bodhisattvas that protect children and pilgrims from harm, and it makes for such a mysterious vibe, especially as there’s usually nobody else around. Locals and devotees knit red hats and make red bibs for the statues, as red is seen as a protective colour in Japan, and it helps make them look even more photogenic.

That’s likely all you’ll have time for with a day in Nikko, so then it’ll be time to either head to your accommodation or journey back to Tokyo. If you’re feeling peckish on the walk back through town, we had some great takoyaki from Takoyaki Japan.
Day Six: Welcome to Traditional Kanazawa!
Kanazawa ended up being my stand-out destination in Japan.

What a wonderful little city, where you can wander through former samurai and geisha districts, admire one of the best Japanese gardens in the country, eat some truly spectacular seafood, and learn more about the history, culture, and crafts of Japan.

Knowing the backstory of Kanazawa helps explain how this city ended up with such a traditional vibe. This part of the country was ruled by the wealthy Maeda family for almost 300 years, and they became major patrons of Japanese culture. Their priority was funding and promoting Japanese gardens, tea ceremonies, Noh theatre, and other traditional crafts. It also helps that Kanazawa managed to avoid much of bombings of WWII, so quite a lot of its historic architecture survived to this day.

Kanazawa is located on the west coast of Japan, and it takes two and a half hours to get there on the Shinkansen from Tokyo. If you decided to spend the night in Hakone, the simplest route is to take the Tokaido Shinkansen to Tokyo and change to the Hokuriku Shinkansen to Kanazawa, but it does mean forfeiting your return train to Shinjuku that’s included in the Hakone Free Pass. If you spent the night in Nikko, you’ll want to travel to Omiya, then onwards to Kanazawa. It takes roughly four-and-a-half to five hours to get to Kanazawa from both places.
Aim to arrive in Kanazawa by around lunchtime, if possible, and you’ll be able to have the best introduction to the local seafood. Yep, Omicho Market has got to be the first place on your itinerary!

So, Omicho Market is the oldest and largest in Kanazawa, with just under 200 stops and restaurants packed inside the covered building. This is the place to come for fresh seafood, and Dave and I still talk about how delicious our kaisendons (a bowl of rice topped with sashimi) were. You’ll find them all over the market, with different restaurants offering different combinations depending on the time of year.
When you’ve had your fill of food, I recommend planning to spend your afternoon exploring the historic districts of the city.

Start with Kazue-machi Chaya, which is one of three geisha districts in Kanazawa. It’s a short walk from Omicho Market, so makes for a logical first stop. This tiny neighbourhood runs alongside the Asano River, with narrow laneways and a dense cluster of traditional wooden buildings. It’s the perfect place for aimless wanderings, as there’s no big attractions here, but plenty of cool architecture.

Higashi Chaya will be your next port of call, which is the most famous of the geisha districts, dating back to the 1820s. The buildings are just as beautiful here, but many have been repurposed into cafes, stores, and teahouses, and so there’s more tourists to contend with, too. If you’re interested in seeing how these buildings would have once looked, head to Geisha House Shima, where you’ll be able to wander through preserved rooms from the 1820s, seeing where geishas would have entertained their clients, and checking out the traditional furnishings and decorations that would have been displayed at that time.

This is also a good part of town to take a look at Kanazawa’s famous gold leaf crafts. This city produces around 99% of Japan’s gold leaf, if you can believe that, so all of the stores and cafes will be selling golf-leaf everything, from ice creams to chocolates, chopsticks to bowls. There’s tons of workshops in the area, too, so you could try your hand at making gold-leaf chopsticks this afternoon: the perfect souvenir to remind you of Kanazawa!

Once you’ve had enough, wander back towards the Asano River. The area around Kazue-machi is particularly lovely in the late afternoon, and if you’re here towards sunset, the old wooden buildings take on a completely different atmosphere once the lights start coming on.

For the evening, head back towards central Kanazawa for dinner. This would be a good night to try something other than sushi, such as Kanazawa oden, so you get to experience a little more of the local food scene beyond the seafood you had for lunch. And when you’re done eating, consider stopping at Oyama Shrine on your way back. Its unusual gate combines Japanese, Chinese, and European influences, and it’s illuminated after dark, making it a good little nighttime stop before heading back to your room.

Where to stay in Kanazawa: We had a hard time choosing where to stay in Kanazawa because every property looked so cosy and inviting. In the end, we settled on this minimalist, modern set-up — it was great value for money for Japan! It’s in a great location, right outside Omicho Market, and within walking distance to Kanazawa Castle and Kenroku-en Garden, so you’re really staying in the heart of it all. I recommend signing up for the traditional Japanese breakfast, as you’ll likely not have had anything else like it before! There’s also an onsen and laundry facilities, and the staff were so sweet and kind.
Day Seven: The Kanazawa Main Attractions

Rise and shine! Today, we’re going to waking up bright and early and heading straight to Kenroku-en: Kanazawa’s most famous attraction, said to be one of Japan’s three great gardens. Because of its fame, crowds can grow from late-morning, so visiting first thing brings a totally different feel to the experience. When Dave and I were there, at around 8 a.m., there were only a couple of other people roaming around, and it meant that we felt like we had the complex all to ourselves.

Kenroku-en really is worth visiting. It’s huge, ridiculously pretty, and full of ponds, streams, bridges, old trees, and winding paths. You’ll likely spend at least an hour here, but Dave and I ended up walking around for two because we kept sitting on the benches to soak up more of the scene.

The official website for the gardens has a really useful map that marks all of the attractions on it and suggests a logical route to take you to every one of them. My favourite area was Kasumigaike Pond and the Kotoji-toro lantern that sits on its shores.

When you’ve had your fill of gardens, head over to Kanazawa Castle, which sits directly beside Kenroku-en. This castle was once the home of the aforementioned Maeda family, but as with the vast majority of castles in Japan, it is unfortunately mostly a reconstruction. (Most of the castles in Japan were built from wood then damaged by fires, so of the 200 castles in this country, only 12 of them are true originals!)

Despite this, I still think the castle is well worth exploring. The thick stone walls, wooden buildings, and immaculate grounds give a much better idea of what the original castle complex would have looked like than a single surviving building ever would. You want to enter through Ishikawa-mon Gate, then make your way around Hishi Yagura, Gojukken Nagaya, and Hashizume-mon. I also enjoyed the castle gardens when I expected them to be underwhelming after Kenroku-en. No so!

We’ll head next to Nagamachi, the old Samurai quarter. As the name suggests, this district used to be home to samurai families, and they served the Maeda family that ruled over Kanazawa. Sumarai were essentially Japanese warriors, although after the wars of the 1500s, the vast majority of them had jobs as teachers and government workers, so weren’t spending their days fighting.

As with the geisha district yesterday, it’s possible to visit some of the old residences, with the best one being Nomura Samurai Residence. The house began to the Nomuras, a high-ranking samurai family, and the interior is artsy and intricate; perhaps not what you might expect for a samurai’s home! The garden, in particular, is a highlight and so peaceful to sit in.

Speaking of gardens, directly opposite the residence, you’ll find Senda-ke Garden, a compact, pleasant garden that’s operated by the great granddaughter of one of the last samurais of Japan. Often, she’s the one running tours of the garden, so you’ll be learning the family’s history from someone who grew up hearing about it.

If you enjoyed seeing the Nomura home, there’s a few other samurai residences in this area that are free to visit. Takada Family Samurai House is a restored home that belonged to a middle-ranking samurai family, while Ashigaru Shiryokan is much simpler, as it belonged to ashigaru, who were at the bottom of the samurai class. Visiting all three gives you a glimpse into how differently samurai families lived depending on their status.
Day Eight: Step Back in Time in Takayama
I was such a big fan of lovely Takayama.

This small mountain town is found in the Hida region of Gifu Prefecture, deep in the Japanese alps. People come here for its beautifully preserved old town, traditional sake breweries, Hida beef, and the rural culture of the mountains that surround it.

I think Takayama also pairs really well with Kanazawa because while both destinations have historic neighbourhoods, they have a very different feel. Kanazawa was shaped by the wealthy Maeda family and their love of arts, crafts, and gardens, while Takayama was built around trade, woodworking, and the resources of the Hida mountains.

The result is a town packed full of wooden merchant houses, canals, sake breweries, bustling markets, mountain temples, and excellent places to eat, and it’s all packed into a compact area that you can easily explore on foot.

You want to aim to get to Takayama quite early, as it’s home to a couple of lovely morning markets that only operate until midday, so you should there as soon as you get into town. Miyagawa Morning Market is my favourite, as it runs alongside the river and is full of stalls selling local fruits and vegetables, homemade trinkets, and plenty of snacks — and much of it is seasonal, so you can never guarantee what you’ll find. Head to Jinya-mae Morning Market afterwards, which is right outside our next stop: Takayama Jinya.

This traditional Japanese building was the government office for the Tokugawa shogunate from the 1690s onwards. Yep, this building is old! It’s also completely unique, as it’s the only surviving office of this type in Japan. It takes roughly an hour to explore the whole building, and you’ll get to see the old administrative office and similar.

From Takayama Jinya, the next logical stop is the Sanmachi historic district. So pretty! Rows of dark wooden buildings, full of stores, cafes, and sake breweries. Dave and I spent a couple of hours just strolling along the main road and many quieter side streets, stopping for snacks and sake.

So, yes. Sake! Takayama is known for its high-quality sake, as its made using local mountain water, rice, and in its cold climate. There are several historic breweries in the old town — I recommend Hirase Sake Brewery — and it’s quick and easy to pop in for a tasting if you’re walking by. Hirase specifically charges 1,000 Yen for their 30-minute tasting, but you can sample as many as you like over that time — up to 30!

And, of course, if you eat meat, you have to try the Hida beef. This specific type of beef comes from Japanese Black cows who have been raised in this area, and it’s known for its intense marbling and tenderness.
When the afternoon comes around, you have a few options for how to spend your time: Higashiyama, the Hida Folk Village, or potentially Shirakawa-go.

Higashiyama is a quieter part of Takayama, filled with temples, shrines, forests, and old cemeteries. Conveniently, there’s a Higashiyama Walking Course that leads you to the historic hillside temples and shrines in the town — plan for this to take a couple of hours, then spend the rest of your afternoon strolling back through Takayama’s old town and wandering along the canals.

You could also opt to check out the Hida Folk Village. This open-air museum is just outside of central Takayama, and is a complex of 30 traditional buildings from the Hida region — many of which have been relocated to the village to show what traditional mountain village life would have looked like.

If you were feeling ambitious, you could take an afternoon trip to the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Shirakawa-go, where you’ll find a secluded village full of traditional gassho-style homes with steep thatched roofs that keeps the snow off in colder months. It’s just under an hour away by bus, and you’ll want to spend around three hours exploring everything there. It can be done in an afternoon, then, but you wouldn’t have time for much else.

Where to stay in Takayama: In Takayama, we stayed in a small, locally-run guesthouse in the centre of town. It felt like particularly good value for Japan, as it was one of the few places we stayed that you could describe as spacious! It even had a kitchen and washing machine. The beds were comfortable and the hotel was within walking distance of everywhere, including the train station. It was quiet, the staff were lovely, and overall, it made for a comfortable stay!
Day Nine: Check Out the Highlights of Northern Kyoto

Welcome to Kyoto! Welcome to… the masses! Yes, Kyoto is undoubtedly going to be the busiest destination you’ll visit in Japan, but try not to let the crowds get to you: they’re here for a reason and that reason is that Kyoto is wonderful, historic, and packed full of temples.

Now, getting to Kyoto from Takayama takes roughly three hours by train, with a change at Nagoya station. I’d aim for the 8 a.m. Hida 4 Limited Express to Nagoya, as that will get you in to Kyoto just after 11 a.m., still giving you plenty of time to see everything. And I’d encourage you to enjoy the ride, too! The journey between Takayama and Nagoya is far from speedy, but you’ll spend your time cruising around mountain scenery, so it’s a particularly photogenic one.

Once you’ve reached Kyoto, head over to Gionkoh to drop off your bags. This cosy guesthouse’s location is one of the reasons I recommend staying there: you’re right in the heart of southern Higashiyama, which is one of my favourite Kyoto neighbourhoods. We’ll spend today both exploring this area and neighbouring Gion.

We’ll start be heading straight over to Kodai-ji: a beautiful Zen temple in the heart of Higashiyama. The temple complex dates back to 1606, and was established by a woman called Nene, who built it to celebrate her husband after his death. The real reason why we’re stopping here, though, is to see its beautiful gardens. The entrance fee is a little steeper than other temples in the area, but that also helps to keep the crowds down and create a more peaceful atmosphere.

Most importantly of all, Kodai-ji has a bamboo forest on its grounds, and it’s way, way less crowded than the packed-to-the-brim Arashiyama Bamboo Forest. I actually don’t recommend heading to Arashiyama’s bamboo forest at all in this itinerary because it’s so chaotic that it’s near-impossible to enjoy. Take your time at the Kodai-ji version instead and you’ll have a much better experience.

Neno-no-Michi Street will be up next, and you’ll be heading south towards Yasaka Pagoda. This historic street is a beauty: lined with townhouses and temples, and that enormous building that you can spot looming in the distance is our next destination.

Welcome to Hokan-ji Temple, which is home to the famous Yasaka Pagoda, one of Kyoto’s most-visited attractions. Now, the temple itself is closed on weekdays, but that’s not as disappointing as it sounds: the real delights come from seeing the photogenic exterior of the buildings. Wander down the side streets surrounding the temple, climb up the cobblestoned slopes, and take photos of it from as many angles as you can.

Ninenzaka and Sannenzaka are the two main streets in this area, and they’re popular for a reason: they’re super beautiful and lined with stores and stalls, and make for a great place to pick up a snack. Kawakatsusohonke Kiyomizuderasandoten offers a variety of different pickles (try the lemon cucumber), Ochanokosaisai Sannenzaka sells tons of cool Japanese spices, Mochi Mochi has excellent mochi, Daikan-yama Candy Apple sells, well, candy apples, and Apple Pie Lab is popular for its freshly baked apple pies that you can grab and go!

Once you’re deep in a sugar coma, you can use that excess energy to power yourself up the hill to the impressive Kiyomizu-dera. This is yet another of Kyoto’s must-see temples, and it’s absolutely enormous, so don’t be surprised if you find yourself spending a couple of hours wandering around. The temple sits on the slopes of Mount Otowa and has panoramic views over Kyoto, as well as tons of little shrines, pagodas, and other viewpoints in every direction.

This one is one of the more impressive temples in Kyoto, and it’s super-old, too: dating back to the year 778 A.D. One of the more unusual attractions is a replica of a spear used by Benkei: a powerful warrior monk from 1100s. This iron pole weighs almost 100 kilograms (200 lbs) and visitors are allowed to try to lift it to see if they’re as strong as Benkei. If you succeed, it brings good fortune your way!

Now, from here, we’ll need to backtrack a bit and head north back through Higashiyama to reach the lovely green space that is Maruyama Park. It doesn’t take much more than 15 minutes and is downhill, so it won’t be too challenging of a walk. This public park is a great one, and perfect for seeking some respite from the crowds. This being Kyoto there is, of course, a few temples you can see while you’re here.

If you’re not yet feeling templed-out, head over to Chion-in, where you’ll find an absolutely enormous temple (home to the largest wooden gate in Japan) that’s free to visit and attracts very few tourists: the travel trifecta! There’s a free shuttle bus that takes you to the top of the hill, but you could also take the steps, which were made famous when they were climbed by Tom Cruise in the movie, the Last Samurai. There’s a couple of gardens in the complex (paid), which are worth a visit, but you could equally just wander around listening to Buddhist chants emanating from the prayer halls.
We’ll next pass through Yasaka Shrine on our way to the neighbourhood of Gion.

From here, you can wander into Gion and spend the rest of your day exploring the old streets around Hanamikoji. This is known as the geisha district of Kyoto, but I’d keep your expectations in check. Kyoto’s geiko (professional entertainers) and maiko (apprentices) aren’t there to provide photographs for tourists, and the city has become increasingly strict about visitors respecting the residents. Instead of making the geishas the focus of your visit, enjoy the architecture, have dinner in the area, and see what Gion is like after dark.
And if you’re staying at Gionkoh, you’ll only be a short walk from your hotel, which is an added bonus after all that walking!

Where to stay in Kyoto: In Kyoto, we stayed in a cosy hotel in the heart of town! The property was in a fantastic location for exploring Kyoto and the bathrooms were nicer than anywhere else we stayed. It’s one of the top-rated guesthouses in the city — while also being one of the cheapest — so when you take that into consideration, I’m convinced you won’t find anywhere better to stay in Kyoto.
Day 10: A Day Trip to Deer-Filled Nara
Nara was one of my highlights of Japan, and a disproportionate amount of my love was due to the deer.

This city was Japan’s first permanent capital, and like Kyoto, it’s chock-a-block with temples and shrines, many of which are more than 1,300 years old. Unlike Kyoto, it’s home to a absolutely unbelievable number of wild deer, all wandering around in the middle of everything. You’ll see them queueing at bus stops, wandering into 7-Elevens, skipping up temple steps, and bowing at cracker-laden tourists.

Once you’ve arrived in town, then, you’ll want to head straight towards Nara Park, where the deer-themed fun and games begin almost immediately. There are deer everywhere, wandering the dirt paths, munching in grass, sleeping beneath trees, hiding in bushes, and generally behaving as though having hundreds of tourists cooing at them is the most average thing in the world.

Official numbers put the number of deer in Nara at around 1,700, and they’re even protected in Japan as Natural Monuments and believed to be holy animals. Famously, they’re known for being the most Japanese of deer, because they’ll bow for food if they suspect you have any crackers to hand (although the bowing wasn’t something I personally witnessed; they were far more likely to nip at my coat pocket in excitement!)
Naturally, you’ll want to feed them.

Throughout Nara Park, you can buy small packets of rice bran crackers (called shika senbei), which are made especially for the deer and are completely safe for them to eat. I recommend wandering through the park until you find a quieter area with a single deer roaming around. It makes for a far calmer experience to only have one deer to feed, as Dave and I struggled to hand out the crackers when we had eight deer surrounding us and trying to get their mouths around them!

Dave and I spent a solid three hours just hanging out in the park, stroking the deer, and taking photos with them, and it was such a magical experience as they were so unbothered by our presence. Today’s itinerary takes you on a loop through the enormous Nara Park, so you’ll encounter deer all throughout the day, so do plan to stop regularly to spend time with them.
Our first main attraction of the day is one of Nara’s many historic temples: Kofuku-ji.

After spending time in Kyoto, you might be feeling well and truly shrined-out by now, and if so, I’ll give you permission to skip over Kofuku-ji. This UNESCO World Heritage Site is located right at the entrance to Nara Park, so you’ll pass by it anyway, and most of the complex is free to visit… but it’s currently undergoing major restoration work until 2030, so it’s not as impressive as it usually is.

There’s two Japanese gardens in Nara: Yoshikien Garden and Isuien Garden. Of the two, I’d recommend Yoshikien, and not just because it’s free (in comparison to Isuien’s 1,200 JPY entrance fee). Because both gardens are a little hidden away, they really don’t attract many crowds, so don’t be surprised if you find yourself sharing the space with less than a dozen people. There’s three main garden designs at Yoshikien: a pond garden, a moss garden, and a tea ceremony garden, and all three are wonderful.

Once you’ve had your fill of miss, you’ll head next to Todai-ji, passing through Nandaimon Gate. And if it looks particularly gigantic to you, yes: this is in fact the largest temple gate in all of Japan!

Inside, the scale remains just as large. The Great Buddha Hall is one of the world’s largest wooden buildings and is home to Japan’s largest bronze Buddha statue. Hilariously, Todai-ji is also where you’ll find the Buddha’s Nostril. Yes, one of the wooden pillars here has a small hole in its base that’s said to be the size of, well, the Buddha’s nostrils. Legend dictates that if you can successfully crawl through the “nostril”, you’ll be guaranteed a long and prosperous life.

While you’re inside the Todai-ji complex, make sure to take the cobblestoned path over to Nigatsudo: a smaller hall perched on the hillside. Not only does it offer up lovely views over Nara, but there’s also free tea for visitors to sip while they’re there.

The walk between Todai-ji and Kasuga Taisha is one of my favourite parts of Nara because the scenery changes so quickly. Before you know it, you’re strolling through a forest lined with hundreds of stone lanterns, with deer popping up between the trees as you pass.

Kasuga Taisha is an important shrine to visit in Nara, because it’s the entire reason why this part of the country is home to so many deer. Briefly, one of the shrine’s deities — Takemikazuchi — arrived in Nara atop a white deer. Deer were then deemed to be sacred messengers of the gods, became Natural Monuments, and killing one was made punishable by death. All around the complex, you’ll find statues of deer.

We’ll now make our way back through Nara Park to the old merchant area of Naramarchi Historic District. Pass by Ukimido Pavilion on your way to the neighbourhood, then prepare yourself for plenty of traditional buildings filled with stores, cafes, and galleries, giving you a glimpse into what this city was like when it was a trading centre rather than the capital of Japan.

Salon Naramachi is a traditional teashop that serves all kinds of teas, sweets, and tasting sets, but the matcha is the star of the show here. You can even get vanilla ice cream with matcha to pour on top! Higashimuki Shopping Street is nearby and is excellent for stocking up on souvenirs and treats — especially mochi! There are so many great mochi and daifuku stores around this neighbourhood. In particular, Kakuozan Fruit Daifuku Benzaiten has mochi filled with any fruit you can think of: pineapple, kiwi, blood orange, persimmon, pear, and more!
Day 11: The Big Sights in Kyoto
For your final day in Kyoto, we’re going to start with one of the city’s most famous sights, then work our way south for one of the most atmospheric.

I’d get up early and make your way to Kinkaku-ji — the Golden Pavilion — aiming to arrive just before it opens at 9 a.m. This is one of those Kyoto attractions where getting there early genuinely makes a difference. It’s one of the city’s biggest tourist draws, and the crowds build as the morning goes on.

The three-storey building is covered in gold leaf and sits beside a pond where its reflection makes the whole thing look almost too perfect to be real. There’s an interesting bit of history behind it, too.

You don’t need half a day here. The main viewing route through the grounds is fairly short, although I’d allow around an hour so you can actually enjoy the garden rather than taking one photo and immediately joining the exit queue.
Once you’ve finished at Kinkaku-ji, continue to Ryoan-ji, which is close enough that you can walk between the two.

The route follows Kinukake-no-Michi, a road linking several of Kyoto’s famous temples in this part of the city. Ryoan-ji is famous for its Zen rock garden, where fifteen rocks are arranged across white gravel. The slightly bizarre part is that you can’t see all fifteen at once from any angle.

Nobody knows for certain who designed the garden or exactly what it was intended to represent, which means you can sit there staring at it for ten minutes and come to your own conclusion. The temple grounds are much larger than the famous garden, with ponds, trees and moss-covered paths, so don’t make the mistake of visiting the rock garden and immediately leaving.
If you’re particularly interested in temples, you can add Ninna-ji to this section of the day. It’s nearby and makes sense geographically, but I wouldn’t make it essential.
Have lunch around the Ryoan-ji area before heading south.
Next up is Fushimi Inari Taisha, the famous Shinto shrine covered in thousands of bright orange torii gates.

This is where I’d deliberately go against the standard Kyoto advice and save it for the late afternoon. The shrine itself doesn’t close, and your experience is going to improve dramatically as you get farther away from the entrance and the crowds thin out.
The first few rows of torii are going to be packed. Don’t let that put you off.
Keep walking.

The gates continue for kilometres up Mount Inari, with smaller shrines, stone fox statues, forest paths and occasional viewpoints appearing as you climb. The complete loop is around four kilometres and takes roughly two hours, so you don’t need to reach the summit to get the full experience.

Personally, I’d aim to arrive around an hour or two before sunset and keep walking until the light starts to fade. The further you go, the quieter it becomes, and by the time you’re high up on the mountain, the manic crowds from the entrance can feel like they’re miles away.
Day 12: Hiroshima and Miyajima Island

Get your day started early because we’ve got a lot of ground to cover. You’ll be heading to Hiroshima today and the best way to get there is via the Shinkansen bullet train. There’s plenty of departures running throughout the day, so there’s no need to panic about getting to Kyoto Station at a certain time. However, it does take slightly over 90 minutes to get there, and we’ll only have one day to explore, so earlier is better!

Some visitors to Japan wonder if it’s necessary to go to Hiroshima; let’s just say it’s not the most cheerful of travel experiences! However, in my opinion, Hiroshima is so important to visit. Not only will you get to fully educate yourself on the horrors that took place here, but you’ll also be able to witness the city’s incredible strength and resilience.

Hiroshima in 2026 is so much more than its past. It’s a vibrant, modern — even hipster — city with excellent food and warm locals. It’s inspiring to witness first-hand how the destination has grown and evolved over the past 80 years. You’ll get a lot out of your visit, I think — I certainly did.
I recommend aiming for the Nozomi 77 Shinkansen, which leaves from Kyoto Station at 7:40 a.m. With no changes along the route, it gets you to Hiroshima by 9:20 a.m.

You can use Google Maps’ public transport information to get from your Kyoto hotel to Kyoto station via the bus — or take an Uber — and rather than having breakfast in a cafe, I recommend grabbing some snacks from a 7-11 at the station to help save on time.

Hiroshima’s train station is located roughly three km, or two miles, from the city’s main landmarks, so I don’t recommend leaving your luggage in the station while you explore. Instead, do as I did and venture first to your hotel to drop your bags; your accommodation should be close to the centre of town. I stayed in this capsule hotel — my first time in one! — and loved it. It was just a three minute walk to Peace Memorial Park, which is where our explorations begin.

Start off by giving yourself several hours to wander the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum. It’s undeniably intense and a difficult place to visit, but you need to go in order to fully understand what took place in this city.

After a quick lunch in Hiroshima, hit the rails and take the train and ferry out to nearby Miyajima Island. It’s a place for respite after a heavy morning of sightseeing, and while you’re there, you can swoon over the wild deer that roam the island, snack on street food, and take selfies in front of the famous Great Torii of the Itsukushima Shrine — you’ll probably have seen this in Japan guidebooks. Most visitors love the laid back vibe of Miyajima.

Head back to Hiroshima for dinner and tuck into a delicious plate of okonomiyaki. Hiroshima’s version of this savoury Japanese pancake is filled with yakisoba noodles, and is the ultimate in comfort food. Definitely make sure to try this while you’re in town so that you can compare it to the Osakan version at your next stop.

Where to stay in Hiroshima: In Hiroshima, we opted for a capsule-style hostel because I didn’t want to leave the country without trying one. Fortunately, we found ourselves in a room with only two other people staying there, so our capsule room with 20-odd beds was light on snorers. The owner of this place was ridiculously lovely, and it was in walking distance of all of the attractions. Really great bathrooms, a fun common area, and a cheap price. I would have stayed another night!
Day 13: Start Eating Everything in Osaka

Wake up bright and early on day 14 and spend a couple of hours wandering through Hiroshima before checking out of your hotel and heading to Osaka. I used this time to stroll through Shukkei-en Garden, visit the Children’s Peace Monument, and take one final wander through Peace Memorial Park.

Onwards! Osaka ended up being my favourite city in Japan, and that’s primarily because it’s where you go to eat. I had one of the best meals of my life in Osaka, and every single thing I ate felt like it was on the verge of life-changing. Dramatic? Always. But man, I love the food in Japan.

After grabbing some lunch, head straight to the city’s most famous attraction: Osaka Castle. If you’re tight on cash, you don’t need to pay to head into the interior, but it does have a pretty great view over the city from the top floor. It’s one of the prettiest castles in Japan, so even sitting outside and taking photos of the shimmering specks of gold feels like a worthwhile activity.

Spend your first evening exploring Dotonbori by night. This vibrant, bustling neighbourhood, and the flashing lights at night are exactly what you’re picturing Japan to be like. Head to Hanamaruken Namba Houzenji for a bowl of pork rib ramen for dinner because it was one of the best meals of my life.

If you’re as much of a foodie as I am, you might want to opt to take this three-hour walking food tour of Osaka while you’re in town. You’ll get to sample 10 of the best local dishes, like takoyaki and yakitori, and two local drinks. The tour covers a whole range of eating establishments, leading you from a street stall to a market, introducing you to a classic Japanese restaurant and izakaya, and finishing off with a secret local hangout.

Where to stay in Osaka: I rounded off my time in Japan with a little bit of a treat, opting for this four-star hotel that offered a ton of freebies. It’s all about the onsen here — it’s open all day and is simply beautiful. After you’ve finished your daily bathe, there’s free ice cream to eat, free comics to read, massage chairs to relax in, and even free ramen to slurp on. Yes, really! It was in a great location for Osaka — just a couple of blocks from the nearest metro station. The decor was calming and traditional; the perfect way to say goodbye to Japan.
Day 14: the South of Osaka

Yesterday, we dedicated our explorations to the northern side of this fabulous city, so today, it’s time to head south. This part of Osaka is home to some of my favourite attractions in the city, and subsequently is where most of the tourists opt to hang out, too. Don’t let that deter you, though, as there’s a reason why this area of town is so popular, and once you leave Dotonbori, it’s easy to get away from the crowds.
Ah, Dotonbori.

This lively Osakan neighbourhood is so much fun to explore; famous for its numerous bars and restaurants, all of which are attempting to draw in customers by brandishing the most over-the-top facades in your face.

If you opted to stay in my my recommended hotel, Dotonbori is a short walk away. Prepare yourself for a sea of colour, and get your phone ready to start taking photos! These colourful shopfronts are so iconically Japan that I think I ended up taking a photo of every single one I passed.

While you’re in the area, make sure to duck away from the main street to check out the city’s beloved Glico Sign. This is actually an advert for a Japanese candy brand, and the running man depicted on the billboard has been in this location from 1935 until present day. These days, it’s become an unofficial symbol of Osaka, so you can’t visit the city without catching a glimpse of it.

We’ll head next to Denden Town, which is the anime district of Osaka, similar to Akihabara in Tokyo. I actually preferred Denden Town, as I thought the stores/attractions were more diverse and there were fewer people crowding in the street.

To make your way there from the Glico sign, head to Namba Walk via Hozenji Mizukake Fudoson Temple. This humble temple is a lovely one and really quite unusual, as there’s a moss-covered statue of Fudo Myoo (a deity in Japan) that you can pour water atop while making a wish.

Once you get to Namba Walk, you’ll wonder if it goes on forever. This is an unbelievably lengthy underground shopping mall filled with interesting stores and restaurants. You can take a walk aboveground, of course, but Namba Walk is both air conditioned for the summer months and undercover for the rainy months, so I usually take the subterranean option.
You’ll want to walk as far as Kuromon Market, where you’ll find some of the best seafood in town, then a little further from that, you’ll find the eclectic Nipponbashi Denden Town.

Here, the stores sell anything that may appeal to those with nerdy tendencies. Think: gaming rigs, customisable PCs, pachinko arcades, claw machines, anime and manga, Pokemon cards, collectibles and figurines, and games for every console from your childhood.

Dave and I really enjoyed browsing the computers at Sofmap Namba, as they had so many incredible machines and components on display. Transparent cases lighting up in neon colours while an anime character lounges on a sofa inside? Only in Japan!

The Super Potato retro games store on Ota Road is particularly fun if you love gaming. This is where you come to buy games and consoles from throughout the ages. Nintendo 64s, Gameboys, the original Playstation, Sega Dreamcasts, and more. As a 90s kid, walking around here was so nostalgic and it took a lot of effort for me not to buy all the games from my childhood!

Take your time meandering through the streets of Den Den, then once you’ve had your fill of neon for the day, wander south to the Tsutenkaku Tower. If you’re wondering, yes, the design of this tower was inspired by the Eiffel Tower!

Now, I don’t actually recommend heading inside the tower itself, as the queues are often long (sometimes as much as 90 minutes to get to the top!) and we’re going to be heading to a more impressive observation tower later. If you’re a thrill-seeker, however, you might enjoy tower’s the Dive and Walk experience, where you jump off of a plank on the side of the tower, 40 metres up. You’re wearing a harness so it ends up being kind of like a slowed-down jump down to the ground.
Once you’ve taken your photos of the tower, stroll past Tennoji Zoo to check out two great temples: Isshin-ji Temple and Shitenno-ji Temple.

Isshin-ji is home to one of the most interesting temple gates I’ve ever seen. It turns out the temple’s head priest is an architect and he designed this unique steel, concrete, and glass structure at the entrance to the complex. It looks like something you’d see in a modern art museum! But that’s not the main reason why I recommend visiting. Inside, you’ll find a collection of Bone Buddha statues, which have been built from the cremated remains of hundreds of thousands of Osakan residents in a practice that dates back to the 1880s! You can’t take photos of the statues, unfortunately, but they’re definitely worth seeing while you’re there.
It’s a short walk over to Shitenno-ji, which is claimed by some to be the first Buddhist temple built in Japan.
And That’s How to Spend Two Weeks in Japan!

And there you have it! This is exactly how I would recommend spending your first two weeks in Japan. For us, it was the perfect itinerary: there wasn’t too much movement, I got to experience the big cities, smaller towns, and beautiful landscapes, and see all the world-class attractions that makes Japan so wonderful.
Now, the only thing left to do is book those plane tickets and start counting down the days until you touch down in Tokyo!
If you’ve been to Japan before, what would you have done differently?
